challenges.name: lock-contention-quiz
challenges.title: Who is waiting for whom?
challenges.description: Three pieces of evidence from CodeDev lock incidents: a migration that froze the enrollments table, a deadlock between two jobs, and a row locked with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

questions.question:
At 14:02 a deploy ran a migration and the enrollments API started to time out. The on-call engineer ran this on PostgreSQL 16:

SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type AS wtype, now() - xact_start AS xact_age,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 52) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'codedev' AND xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY xact_start;

  pid  |        state        | wtype  | xact_age |  blocked_by | query
-------+---------------------+--------+----------+-------------+------------------------------------------------------
 41207 | idle in transaction | Client | 00:23:41 | {}          | SELECT id, status FROM enrollments WHERE user_id = $1
 52310 | active              | Lock   | 00:00:48 | {41207}     | ALTER TABLE enrollments ADD COLUMN source text
 52388 | active              | Lock   | 00:00:47 | {52310}     | SELECT id, course_id FROM enrollments WHERE user_id
 52391 | active              | Lock   | 00:00:47 | {52310}     | INSERT INTO enrollments (user_id, course_id, status)
(... 214 more rows, all blocked_by {52310})

Statement: "The API queries are waiting because ALTER TABLE is rewriting the enrollments table; they will continue once the rewrite finishes, so the fix is to make the rewrite faster."
questions.explanation: False. The ALTER TABLE is not doing any work: its wait_event_type is Lock and pg_blocking_pids shows it is itself blocked by pid 41207, a session that ran a SELECT on enrollments 23 minutes ago and never committed (idle in transaction). That SELECT still holds an ACCESS SHARE lock until its transaction ends. ALTER TABLE needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, so it waits, and every later query on the table, even a plain SELECT, queues behind the waiting ALTER because its requested lock conflicts with theirs. Adding a nullable column without a default does not rewrite the table at all. The fix is to end the root blocker (fix the code that leaves the transaction open, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout) and to run migrations with SET lock_timeout = '3s' and a retry, so a DDL statement that cannot get its lock gives up instead of freezing the table. The misconception is to blame the statement at the head of the visible queue instead of following blocked_by to the root.

questions.question:
Two jobs update the same enrollments. The bundle job activates a bundle's enrollments in the order the bundle lists them; the refund job deactivates them in the order the payment provider sends them. Server log (PostgreSQL 16):

ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 6012 waits for ShareLock on transaction 9120443; blocked by process 6087.
        Process 6087 waits for ShareLock on transaction 9120441; blocked by process 6012.
        Process 6012: UPDATE enrollments SET status = 'active' WHERE id = 3002
        Process 6087: UPDATE enrollments SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE id = 1001
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (1840,7) in relation "enrollments"

Earlier in the same transactions, process 6012 had updated id 1001 and process 6087 had updated id 3002.

Statement: "If both jobs lock the rows they will change in ascending id order before updating them, for example with SELECT id FROM enrollments WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE, these two jobs can no longer deadlock with each other on these rows."
questions.explanation: True. A deadlock needs a cycle: 6012 holds 1001 and wants 3002, while 6087 holds 3002 and wants 1001. When every transaction acquires its row locks in the same global order (here ascending id), the one that gets 1001 first also gets to 3002 first and the other simply waits, so no cycle can form. SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE takes the locks in that order up front. Waiting for ShareLock on a transaction is how PostgreSQL shows a wait for a row lock held by that transaction. Retrying on SQLSTATE 40P01 is still good practice, but it handles deadlocks; a consistent lock order removes this one. The misconception is that deadlocks are random bad luck that only retries can address.

False. A plain SELECT never waits for row locks in PostgreSQL: thanks to MVCC it reads the last committed version of the row and returns at once, here the status before A's update. What does wait for A's FOR UPDATE lock is another writer or locking read on the same row: UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE. The real problem in this code is different: A holds a row lock for the whole 8-second network call, so a second checkout or the refund job for enrollment 42 would wait that long. Do the external call outside the transaction, or lock as late as possible. The misconception is that a lock on a row blocks everyone who reads it.
